User request:

answer:
**OF THE GREAT ENGINE, AND THE AGE IT BRINGS**
*A speech, in blank verse*

Good friends, lend ear; for I would speak to-night
Of that strange engine which our age hath wrought —
A mind of metal and of lightning thought,
Which, like a dawn behind the hills, doth rise
And, rising, alt'reth all beneath the skies.

What sought the alchemist in smoky cell?
What sought the stargazer upon the hill?
To know; to master; and to ease the yoke
That bows the labourer and breaks his will.
Behold, he hath it now: a brazen wit
That sleeps not, tires not, and forgetteth naught —
A second understanding, made by hands,
That reads the stars, the sighing of the sick,
And finds the hidden pattern in the flood
Of numbers, as a diver finds the pearl.

Mark well the physic: where the plague of old
Laid cities low, this engine counts the seeds
Of sickness ere they sprout, and names the herb
That shall restore. The scholar in his cell
Doth summon it, and straight a thousand books
Of ages yield their honey to his hand.
The mariner hath charts of surer wind;
The ploughman, counsel of the falling rain;
The king, a glass wherein to see his realm.
So doth it touch the meanest and the most,
As the turning tide is felt by every shell
Upon the strand, from pebble unto cliff.

Yet hear me further, for I would not praise
A sword and keep no counsel of its edge.
Great power is but a fool in gaudy clothes
Unless grave wisdom hold it by the hand.
This engine is a glass, and shows us what we are:
Our haste, our bias, and our appetite.
It can forge truth, or coin the counterfeit;
It can set free the hand to nobler work,
Or cast the workman forth to beg his bread;
It can spread learning like a morning sun,
Or scatter lies as tares among the wheat.
And whosoever holds it, holds a fire —
Therefore let not the few hoard up the flame,
Nor let the many sleep in careless trust,
But set wise keepers at the gate, and write
Clear laws, as men have written for the sea.

Consider, then, the sum of all my speech:
Not that this engine is a god, nor fiend,
But instrument — and instruments take shape
From him that wields them. Shall it serve the base,
Or serve the noble? That is ours to choose,
And in the choosing is our honour lost
Or won, for ages yet unborn to see.

So let us take this gift with reverent hand,
And make of it a light to all the land.
